record.paper_title: Ductile-to-brittle transition and yielding in soft amorphous materials: perspectives and open questions
record.context_brief: wall slip and near-wall plasticity in transients
record.original_question: During transient flows of soft amorphous materials, especially aging systems, how are wall slip and plastic events near the wall related, should comparisons of aging time with near-wall plastic-event rates replace length-scale comparisons, and how can wall slip be suppressed, reduced, or tuned in dense suspensions and colloidal gels?

evidence.quote: In that case, comparing two characteristic time scales, e.g., the aging time and the inverse of the plastic event rate near the wall, could be more relevant than comparing two length scales. Moreover, this picture prompts us to better understand the link between wall slip and plastic events in dilute systems, for these two concepts could be deeply related.

Besides these fundamental considerations, addressing wall slip should help develop global strategies to suppress, reduce, and even tune wall slip for a broad variety of soft materials, from dense suspensions to colloidal gels, in steady-state flow as well as in transient regimes.

artifact.category_tag: wall slip and plasticity in soft amorphous materials
artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a soft amorphous material (e.g., a dense colloidal suspension, a colloidal gel, or another aging yield-stress fluid) confined between two solid walls and subjected to a transient shear flow. Such a material exhibits localized, irreversible rearrangements ("plastic events") whose rate per unit volume near the wall can be denoted r_w(t), and it may also display wall slip, i.e., a discontinuity v_s(t) between the velocity of the material adjacent to the wall and the velocity of the wall itself. If the material is aging, let t_a denote its age (the time elapsed since preparation/rejuvenation).

Address the following:

(a) Establish a quantitative relation, in the transient regime, between the wall-slip velocity v_s(t) and the near-wall plastic-event rate r_w(t). In particular, determine whether wall slip in dilute or aging systems can be derived from (or is equivalent to) a concentration of plastic events in a boundary layer adjacent to the wall.

(b) Formulate a criterion for the onset and magnitude of wall slip during transients based on the comparison of the time scales t_a and 1/r_w(t), and compare it with criteria based on the comparison of length scales (such as a near-wall cooperativity length versus the gap or a particle size). Determine under which physical conditions the time-scale comparison supersedes the length-scale comparison as the controlling criterion.

(c) Provide constructive strategies — through surface chemistry, boundary roughness, confinement geometry, particle interactions, or imposed flow protocols — to suppress, reduce, or precisely tune v_s(t) in both steady-state and transient flow regimes, applicable across the range from dense suspensions to colloidal gels.
artifact.status_search_result: The question is posed as an open perspective on transient rheology of soft amorphous solids. No comprehensive theoretical link between wall slip and near-wall plastic-event rates in aging systems, nor a universal suppression/tuning strategy, appears to be established in the literature; recent works continue to investigate slip mechanisms in suspensions and gels without providing a unified answer.
